title: Grosshau falls by moonlight

facts.text: Since 16 November 1944 the US 4th Infantry Division had been fighting east through the Hürtgen Forest toward Düren and the Roer River. Col. Charles T. "Buck" Lanham's 22nd Infantry was aimed at Grosshau, a village in a clearing on the forest's eastern edge.

A first try on 25 November failed. Only three tanks and a tank destroyer got out of the woods with the infantry, German antitank gunners in Grosshau picked off the tanks, and artillery drove the men back into the forest.
In two more days of limited fighting the 22nd Infantry suffered over 250 casualties, and two of its companies had fewer than fifty men each in the line.

For 29 November Lanham planned a wide flanking march through the woods to the north to seize the ridge behind Grosshau, hoping the Germans in the village would then give up without another charge across open fields.

German shelling delayed the start. Just before noon the division chief of staff, Col. Richard S. Marr, stepped in, in the division commander's name, and directed that Grosshau be taken that day. That meant a head on assault.

Lanham's only free battalion was Major Blazzard's 2nd Battalion, as weak as any in the division. Within an hour one company with two tanks and a tank destroyer attacked down the road from the west. Within fifteen minutes the infantry was pinned in the open and both tanks had fallen to German assault guns.

Eight more tanks tried to swing around to the southwest. Two hit mines at once, and the rest could not get out of the woods through the minefields and bog. The sun was going down on what the official history calls an abject failure.

Then Lanham's flanking force cut the Grosshau to Gey highway, and as night came one battalion emerged on the ridge northeast of the village, behind the defenders. Tanks and tank destroyers used the dusk to reach the stalled infantry and rolled into Grosshau firing. Resistance collapsed in minutes.
By the light of burning buildings and a moon, the first moon the division had seen since entering the forest, the infantry mopped up. More than a hundred Germans surrendered.

Ernest Hemingway, covering the war for Collier's, was with Lanham's regiment. The two had met in Normandy, and Hemingway followed him into the Hürtgen, reaching the regimental command post on 15 November and seldom leaving his side.
Hemingway later drew on the Hürtgen for his novel Across the River and Into the Trees. Lanham was one of the models for its hero, Colonel Cantwell.

photoNote: Tier: green. Weary infantrymen rest on a slope in the Hürtgen Forest, 18 November 1944: Pfc. Maurice Berzon, S/Sgt. Bernard Spurr and S/Sgt. Harold Glessler, Company I, 3rd Battalion, 8th Infantry, 4th Infantry Division. US Army Signal Corps photo SC 196619, from the National Archives via the Signal Corps Archive on Flickr and Wikimedia Commons, public domain (US Army work). Saved 1920 x 1567 from the Commons 1920 px thumbnail (original 3713 x 3031). Chosen for the faces: three exhausted men, rifles in hand, which carries the cost of the Hürtgen better than a forest scene. Caveat: it shows the 4th Division's 8th Infantry, not Lanham's 22nd, eleven days before Grosshau; the caption must not call them 22nd Infantry men. I could not find a NARA photo of Grosshau itself or of Lanham. Runner up: SC 196621, squad leader Mike Ala on a handie talkie radio, Hürtgen, 18 November 1944 (Commons). Rejected: the well known photo of Pfc. Benny Barrow aided by medics (Commons 49829370178), because its embedded metadata credits Time and Life Pictures/Getty.

declassified.fact: The admiration ran both ways. Lanham wrote to his wife, Mary, that Hemingway was "probably the bravest man I have ever known." Hemingway called Lanham "the finest and bravest and most intelligent military commander I have known."

sources.title: David Sears, When Ernest Hemingway Went From Writer to Fighter, World War II magazine, June 2020 (HistoryNet)

film.record: U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2798 (NARA 16601), "Tank firing, Grosshau; AA battery knocks out buzz bombs, near Mansfield, Belgium; rocket launcher on L-4; 4.5 rockets, Hurtgen Forest"
film.license: U.S. government work (Army Signal Corps), public domain; NARA marks the 111-ADC series Restricted Possibly as a blanket note
film.shot_notes: Whole reel, 8 min 56 s, silent (the shot card says silent; the file has only hiss). NOON (this card): the 4.5 inch rocket batteries in the Hurtgen Forest, slated on screen "Barth D, 29 Nov 1944, 4.5 rockets, Hurtgen Forest" at 07:27 (avoid the slate itself): 06:39 to 06:57 truck mounted multiple rocket launchers in a forest clearing, crews at the racks; 06:58 to 07:26 a crewman on the field phone giving fire orders (faces, close); 07:30 to 07:57 launchers in the clearing firing, smoke; 07:58 to 08:24 the trucks move along the forest edge to new positions. Open on the launchers at 07:30 (smoke and firing) or 06:39. Tanks firing at Grosshau (00:08 to 01:40) belong to Monday's No. 104; the AA battery (01:55 to 04:12) to No. 103; the L-4 rockets (04:15 to 06:38) to Tuesday's No. 109. Do not reuse any of those here.
film.date_note: The shot card dates the rocket stretch 30 Nov 1944 but the slate chalked on screen reads 29 Nov 1944; either way it is the Hurtgen Forest on the day Grosshau fell or the day after. Caption it as U.S. Army film of rocket batteries in the Hurtgen Forest, 29 to 30 Nov 1944, not as Grosshau itself.
